extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, research funders, and academic researchers involved in peer review policy
extracted.subtask_description: Policies and practical criteria for transforming volunteer peer review into a paid, trained, certified professional referee system for scientific journals. Covers reviewer training/certification, team-based review, funding models, independence safeguards, and operational rollout (pilots, curricula).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer compensation / paid professional referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviewers should be paid and transformed into professional referees rather than relying on voluntary goodwill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The volunteer model is described as broken; funding could come from publishers (given high profit margins) or research funders. Options include employing internal reviewers or maintaining externally contracted paid reviewers. A suggested initial funding mechanism is a small allocation (e.g., 2–3%) of article processing charges or subscription fees. Funders (NIH, ERC, Wellcome Trust) could mandate professional review for funded research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training and certification of reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must undergo specific training and certification to learn to evaluate scientific merit, methodology, statistics, and ethics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certification analogous to sports officiating would teach reviewers to identify methodological flaws, statistical errors, and ethical concerns. Learned societies could establish training curricula. Training is central to reconceptualising reviewing as a professional role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specialist assistants (team-based review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific referees should collaborate with specialist assistants—statisticians, methodology experts, reference checkers—similar to assistant referees and VAR in sports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A team approach ensures comprehensive evaluation and distributes workload. Examples: statistical reviewers for analyses, reference checkers for citation integrity, methodology experts for experimental design critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thoroughness and comprehensiveness of evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews must comprehensively assess scientific merit, methodology, statistical soundness, and ethical considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional reviewers are expected to identify methodological flaws, statistical errors, and ethical concerns rather than provide superficial or generic comments. Thorough, specialist-backed evaluations are emphasized as necessary for quality control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of review delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews should be delivered promptly because reviewing would be a paid professional responsibility rather than an afterthought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professionalisation is argued to produce timely, thorough assessments since reviewing would be a job rather than squeezed between other academic duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match reviewer expertise to manuscript content
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign reviewers whose expertise aligns with the manuscript's topic and methods to avoid 'not my expertise' or irrelevant critiques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialist assistants and a professional reviewer pool help ensure expertise alignment, reducing irrelevant comments (e.g., critiquing wet-lab needs for theoretical work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid AI-generated, generic, or detached reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: AI use in review is forbidden and must be actively detected and prevented because AI-generated reviews often are generic, excessively long, and detached from the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors report hallmarks of AI reviews: excessive length (often >3,000 words vs preferred 500–1,000), many long bullet lists (20+ items), perfect grammar with no minor errors, and generic comments not specific to the paper's content. Enforcement mechanisms are currently lacking and must be established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness and appropriate review length
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews should be focused and appropriately concise (suggested ~500–1,000 words) rather than overly verbose (>3,000 words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive verbosity is flagged as an AI hallmark and an anti-pattern; concise, manuscript-specific feedback is preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence and conflict-of-interest safeguards for paid reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Compensation structures must preserve reviewer independence and neutrality despite payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the sports analogy: referees are paid by leagues, not competing teams, and remain neutral through professional protocols and oversight. Payment should be structured and overseen to avoid compromising impartiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability and oversight structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish accountability, oversight, and professional protocols to maintain review quality and neutrality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeled on sports officiating with systematic oversight, these structures would monitor reviewer performance, enforce standards (including AI-use policies), and ensure consistent application of criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable distribution of reviewing workload
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevent over-reliance on a small subset of conscientious reviewers and distribute reviewing labor more fairly across a professional pool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professionalisation and paid roles would reduce the current imbalance where a minority perform most reviews; formal career paths and compensation would encourage broader participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and career development pathways for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Create formal recognition, credentials, and career development opportunities for reviewers so reviewing is a valued professional activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear pathways, certification, and recognition would reframe reviewing from an unwelcome obligation to career-enhancing work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phased implementation and pilots
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce professional review via phased transition: pilot programs at flagship journals, establishment of training curricula, and gradual expansion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start small with pilots to demonstrate value, then scale. Initial funding could come from small APC/subscription percentage allocations or grants for pilot programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishers' financial responsibility given profits
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers—many with high-profit margins—should bear primary responsibility for funding professional review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because publishers profit substantially from scientific publishing, the editorial argues they have a moral and practical obligation to support reviewer compensation rather than leaving it unfunded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic feasibility and concrete funding mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review professionalisation requires clear, feasible funding mechanisms (e.g., percentage of APCs/subscriptions, funder mandates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A concrete proposal: allocate 2–3% of APCs or subscription revenues to fund professional review. Research funders could mandate paid professional review for funded outputs, creating market pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject post-publication review as sole solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-publication critique alone is insufficient to replace robust pre-publication peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-publication review is described as haphazard and non-systematic; thus it cannot substitute for systematic, professional pre-publication review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid perverse incentives (e.g., self-citation) from poor compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Current token-compensation models can incentivize ethically problematic behavior like excessive self-citation and must be remedied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because recognition-only schemes (database access, Publons) are inadequate, they may encourage unethical compensation-seeking behaviors; proper pay and oversight reduce such incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational models: internal vs external reviewer employment
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals may either employ internal professional reviewers or maintain externally contracted paid reviewers; both models are acceptable if standards and oversight are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different journals may choose different operational models depending on resources; both require training, certification, and accountability to ensure consistency.
